title: Weekend jobs with Honey Potter's band on Long Island
summary: Saxophonist Cecil Smith brings Scott, still in high school, to Honey Potter's band for firemen's and policemen's balls.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Well, it so happened that in playing around, I met one of the fellows that was in the band, by the name of Cecil Smith. He was a saxophone player. He became interested in me, I don't know why. He just liked me, that's all. And talking with fellows I'd met, musicians. And he asked me, hey, Scotty, what you doing? You working? I said, no. He says, do you belong (unintelligible)? I said, no. He said, well, that's right, you're too young.

I was still in high school. He said, can you work weekends? I said, oh, yes, sure, sure, sure. He said, well, I'll tell you, you have to come a long way, down on Long Island. He says, but I'll take you out there. He had heard me play, and he said, I could do all right. This fellow was named Honey Potter of Freeport, Long Island. If Honey Potter had been a businessman and had a good education, he could have made a million dollars. He had most of the work out there in Long Island.
See, everything was live music then. There was no radio, and no -- of course, no television. Well, we used to go from Harlem and drive out to Long Island. Honey's wife --

he had a nice house on Bennington Avenue, and his wife, Nellie, she used to cook for us and we'd eat a meal, then we'd drive to where we'd be playing. Mostly it was firemen and policemen's balls. Those people (unintelligible). And, well, it was -- I enjoyed every minute of it.
Honey, he could only play in certain keys, but I knew those keys, and right away, they liked me. So every weekend, there it went, Honey Potter, Honey Potter, Honey Potter.

He played piano. He's a pianist. And he read by ear. But by then, of course, I finally had got a Victrola, and records. And, of course, I got all the records I could get and listened to them, and I had a quick ear. When I'd hear a band playing a number, I had it. That tune was in there, see.
